body:
The Tripitaka

The Buddha's teachings were initially transmitted orally. Buddhist communities subsequently organised them into collections of religious teachings, monastic regulations and philosophical analysis.

The Pali Buddhist canon is known as the Tipitaka, or Tripitaka, meaning 3 baskets.

PitakaPrincipal subject
Vinaya PitakaRules and discipline for the monastic order
Sutta PitakaDiscourses, dialogues and teachings
Abhidhamma PitakaSystematic philosophical and psychological analysis

Other important Buddhist literary works include the Dhammapada, a collection of ethical and philosophical verses; the Jataka stories, which recount previous births of the Buddha; and the Buddhacharita, a Sanskrit account of the Buddha's life composed by Ashvaghosha.

The Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are important Pali chronicles associated with the history of Buddhism in Sri Lanka.

Major Buddhist traditions

Theravada

Theravada means the tradition or teaching of the elders. It preserves the Pali canon and gives particular importance to disciplined practice and the attainment of liberation represented by the ideal of the Arhat. An Arhat is one who has overcome the defilements responsible for rebirth.

Theravada became particularly influential in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, including Myanmar and Thailand.

Mahayana

Mahayana, meaning the Great Vehicle, developed over several centuries. It places special emphasis on the Bodhisattva ideal, in which the pursuit of Buddhahood is motivated by compassion and the welfare of all sentient beings.

Mahayana encouraged important traditions of devotion to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and the production of religious images and new scriptures.

  • Avalokiteshvara is associated with compassion.
  • Manjushri is associated with wisdom.
  • Maitreya is the future Buddha.

Mahayana spread widely through Central and East Asia, particularly to China, Korea and Japan.

Vajrayana

Vajrayana, meaning the Diamond or Thunderbolt Vehicle, developed within the wider Mahayana Buddhist environment. It incorporates esoteric religious teachings, mantras, mandalas, symbolic rituals and guidance from qualified spiritual teachers.

It became particularly influential in Tibet and Himalayan regions.

Hinayana was a historical term used by certain Mahayana writers for other Buddhist schools. It should not be treated as a precise synonym for the surviving Theravada tradition.

Buddhism and Indian art

Buddhist ideas gave rise to important forms of religious architecture and sculpture. Monastic communities required places for residence, meditation and worship, while lay devotees supported the construction of sacred monuments.

  • Stupa: A sacred monument commonly associated with relics, commemoration and worship. Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh is a major example.
  • Chaitya: In Buddhist architectural usage, a place or hall of worship, often containing a stupa.
  • Vihara: A monastery or residential establishment for monks.

Early Buddhist sculptural traditions frequently represented significant events through symbols rather than human images of the Buddha. The Bodhi tree represented enlightenment, the wheel represented the first sermon and the stupa represented final liberation or the sacred presence associated with relics.

Human images of the Buddha subsequently became important in the Gandhara and Mathura artistic traditions. Buddhist narrative art also represented Jataka stories, allowing religious teachings to be communicated visually.

Patronage and transmission

Emperor Ashoka supported Buddhism during the 3rd century BCE. His inscriptions also propagated a broader moral policy known as Dhamma, which encouraged humane conduct, restraint and respect among religious traditions.

During the Kushana period, Kanishka was an important patron of Buddhism. Ashvaghosha is traditionally associated with his court. Monks, scholars, merchants and pilgrims contributed to the spread of Buddhism through commercial routes and monastic networks.

Ashoka's public Dhamma was an ethical policy intended for a diverse population. It was influenced by Buddhism but was not identical to the complete religious doctrine of Buddhism.

Buddhist heritage in Gujarat

Gujarat possesses inscriptions, monastic remains, caves and archaeological sites demonstrating the historical presence of Buddhism.

SiteDistrictSignificance
Girnar rock edictsJunagadhAshokan inscriptions communicating Dhamma
Uparkot, Khapra Kodiya and Baba Pyare cavesJunagadhAncient rock-cut complexes
Khambhalida cavesRajkotBuddhist rock-cut architecture and sculpture
Devni MoriAravalliBuddhist stupa and monastic archaeological remains
Talaja cavesBhavnagarAncient rock-cut religious architecture

The Ashokan inscriptions at Girnar are important for studying the Mauryan Empire and the spread of ethical ideas. The inscriptions use Prakrit written in the Brahmi script.

Prelims focus

  • Vinaya Pitaka contains monastic regulations.
  • Ashvaghosha composed Buddhacharita.
  • Mahayana emphasises the Bodhisattva ideal.
  • Maitreya is the future Buddha; Avalokiteshvara is associated with compassion.
  • Khambhalida is in Rajkot district and Devni Mori is in Aravalli district.
  • Trap: A vihara is a monastery, whereas a chaitya is associated with worship.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 86 and 95–104; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 10, Traders, Kings and Pilgrims, pp. 103–107; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art Part I, chapters on Mauryan and post-Mauryan art; Gujarat Tourism, Buddhist Circuit and Khambhalida Caves, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Buddhist Schools, Sacred Literature and Cultural Heritage

body:
The Tirthankara tradition

Jainism is an ancient Indian religious and philosophical tradition that teaches liberation through self-discipline, right knowledge and the removal of karmic bondage.

A Tirthankara is an enlightened teacher who establishes a path through which others may cross the cycle of worldly existence. Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras in the present half-cycle of cosmic time.

NumberTirthankaraTraditional association
1Rishabhanatha or AdinathaFirst Tirthankara
22NeminathaGirnar pilgrimage tradition
23Parshvanatha4 major vows
24Vardhamana MahaviraSystematic emphasis on 5 vows

Mahavira belonged to a Kshatriya clan connected with the Vajji confederacy. According to Jain tradition, he renounced household life at the age of 30 and attained perfect knowledge after approximately 12 years of ascetic practice.

Mahavira was not the first teacher of Jainism. He was the 24th Tirthankara and an important teacher who strengthened and reorganised an existing tradition.

Jiva, Ajiva and karma

Jain philosophy distinguishes between Jiva, meaning living or conscious substance, and Ajiva, meaning non-living substance.

Jainism accepts the existence of enduring individual souls. Each soul possesses the potential for perfect knowledge, perception and spiritual freedom. However, these qualities are obscured by karmic bondage.

Unlike traditions that understand karma primarily as the moral consequence of action, Jain philosophy also conceives of karma as subtle material particles that become associated with the soul through activity and passions.

Ethical restraint prevents the accumulation of new karmic bondage, while austerity and spiritual discipline help remove accumulated karma. Complete removal of karmic bondage leads to liberation.

The Five Great Vows

The Mahavratas are the 5 great vows observed strictly by Jain monks and nuns. Householders follow corresponding vows in a limited form known as Anuvratas.

  • Ahimsa: Non-injury to living beings.
  • Satya: Truthfulness.
  • Asteya: Abstaining from theft.
  • Brahmacharya: Celibacy for renouncers and sexual restraint for householders.
  • Aparigraha: Non-possession or non-attachment to possessions.

Ahimsa occupies a particularly important position because Jainism recognises life in a wide range of beings, including extremely small forms of life. Jain ethical discipline therefore attempts to minimise harm through careful conduct.

Parshvanatha is traditionally associated with 4 vows, while Mahavira's teaching explicitly recognises Brahmacharya as a separate fifth vow.

The Three Jewels of Jainism

The Jain Triratna consists of 3 interdependent conditions necessary for liberation:

  • Samyak Darshana: Right faith or right perception.
  • Samyak Jnana: Right knowledge.
  • Samyak Charitra: Right conduct.

Knowledge alone is insufficient if conduct continues to produce karmic bondage. Similarly, ethical discipline must be guided by correct understanding.

Anekantavada and Syadvada

Anekantavada is the Jain doctrine that reality has multiple aspects and cannot ordinarily be described completely from a single limited viewpoint.

Syadvada is the method of making qualified statements that recognise the conditions and standpoint under which a claim is valid.

A clay pot may be permanent in the limited sense that its material continues to exist, but impermanent in the sense that its particular shape can be destroyed. The statements concern different aspects of the same object.

These doctrines encourage intellectual restraint and recognition of different perspectives. They do not imply that every contradictory claim is equally correct without qualification.

Digambara and Svetambara traditions

The 2 major Jain traditions differ in certain monastic customs, scriptural traditions and interpretations of spiritual practice.

FeatureDigambaraSvetambara
MeaningSky-cladWhite-clad
Male monastic clothingFull renunciants traditionally practise nudityMonks wear white garments
Scriptural positionDoes not recognise the surviving Svetambara Agamas as the preserved original canonRecognises its transmitted Agama tradition

Both traditions share fundamental Jain principles such as non-violence, karma, spiritual discipline and liberation. Differences also exist within each major tradition.

Jain sacred literature

Jain teachings were preserved in oral traditions and written works composed in Prakrit, Sanskrit and several regional languages.

  • Agamas: Traditional Jain sacred teachings, particularly associated with the Svetambara canonical tradition.
  • Kalpa Sutra: A text containing accounts of Tirthankaras, monastic lineages and religious rules. Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabahu, it is recited during Svetambara Paryushana.
  • Tattvartha Sutra: A systematic exposition of Jain philosophy attributed to Umasvati, also known as Umasvami. It is authoritative across both major Jain traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Rishabhanatha is the 1st, Neminatha the 22nd, Parshvanatha the 23rd and Mahavira the 24th Tirthankara.
  • Jain Triratna consists of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
  • Anekantavada concerns the many-sided nature of reality.
  • Syadvada concerns qualified statements about reality.
  • Tattvartha Sutra is associated with Umasvati or Umasvami.
  • Trap: Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara, not the first Tirthankara.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, pp. 69–72; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 88–89; Jainpedia, Jain Beliefs, Sacred Writings, Tattvartha Sutra and Kalpa Sutra thematic resources, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Jainism: Non-violence, Knowledge and Liberation

body:
Jainism in Gujarat

Jainism established strong religious, literary and cultural traditions in western India, particularly in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Merchant communities supported monks, temples, manuscript libraries and educational activities.

Jain patronage contributed to the development of urban religious institutions, manuscript preservation, sculpture, temple architecture and intellectual life in Gujarat.

Vallabhi and the Jain canon

Vallabhi, also called Valabhi, in present-day Gujarat was an important centre of learning and Jain scholarship.

According to the Svetambara tradition, a council held at Vallabhi during approximately the 5th century CE organised and recorded the surviving Svetambara canonical teachings. The council is traditionally associated with Devardhigani Kshamashramana.

Its importance lies in the preservation of religious knowledge that had previously been transmitted orally. The Digambara tradition does not accept the surviving Svetambara canon as an authentic preservation of the complete original teachings.

Acharya Hemachandra

Acharya Hemachandra was an influential 12th-century Svetambara Jain scholar from Gujarat. He was born at Dhandhuka and became associated with the Chaulukya or Solanki royal court at Anahilapataka, present-day Patan.

He received the patronage of Siddharaja Jayasimha and became an influential religious and intellectual adviser to Kumarapala.

His scholarship extended across grammar, literature, philosophy, history and religious conduct. Important works include:

  • Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana: A major grammatical work dealing with Sanskrit and Prakrit, including Apabhramsha.
  • Trishashti-Shalaka-Purusha-Charitra: Accounts of the 63 great persons recognised in Jain tradition.
  • Yogashastra: A work concerned with Jain ethical and spiritual discipline.

Hemachandra is traditionally honoured with the title Kalikala Sarvajna, reflecting the remarkable breadth of his scholarship.

Important Jain pilgrimage centres

CentreDistrictPrincipal association
Palitana and Shatrunjaya HillBhavnagarAdinatha and extensive Jain temple complexes
GirnarJunagadhNeminatha
TarangaMehsanaImportant Jain pilgrimage and temple architecture
PatanPatanJain scholarship and manuscript preservation

Manuscript culture and painting

Jain religious institutions maintained manuscript libraries, commonly known as Bhandaras or Jnana Bhandaras. Monks, scholars and patrons helped preserve religious texts as well as works on grammar, mathematics, poetry and philosophy.

The illustrated Jain manuscript tradition became an important component of western Indian painting. Manuscripts of the Kalpa Sutra frequently depicted events from the lives of Tirthankaras and other sacred narratives.

Charvaka or Lokayata

Charvaka, also called Lokayata, represents the materialist tradition of ancient Indian philosophy. It rejected Vedic authority and questioned concepts such as an afterlife, ritual merit and an immortal soul.

Perception was regarded as the fundamental reliable source of knowledge. Charvaka thinkers criticised inferences about unseen supernatural realities that lacked adequate experiential support.

Brihaspati is traditionally associated with this school, although its original foundational texts have not survived. Much of the available information comes from accounts and criticisms written by other philosophical traditions. Consequently, the exact views of different Charvaka thinkers cannot always be established with certainty.

The Ajivika tradition

The Ajivikas were an ancient Shramana community particularly associated with Makkhali Gosala, a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira.

Ajivika philosophy is known for its doctrine of Niyati, or destiny. It held that the course of existence was predetermined and could not be fundamentally altered by individual effort.

The Ajivikas received royal patronage during the Mauryan period. Ashoka dedicated certain caves in the Barabar Hills of Bihar to Ajivika ascetics.

As with Charvaka, the original philosophical literature of the Ajivikas has largely been lost, and their teachings are reconstructed primarily from other traditions.

Comparison of major ancient non-Vedic systems

TraditionPrincipal distinctionAssociated figure
BuddhismMiddle Way and cessation of sufferingGautama Buddha
JainismNon-violence and liberation from karmic bondageMahavira
CharvakaMaterialism and emphasis on perceptionBrihaspati, traditionally
AjivikaPredetermined destinyMakkhali Gosala

Prelims focus

  • Vallabhi is associated with the preservation of the Svetambara Jain canon.
  • Hemachandra was associated with Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala.
  • Palitana is associated with Adinatha; Girnar with Neminatha.
  • Charvaka represents the materialist tradition.
  • Makkhali Gosala is associated with Ajivika and Niyati.
  • Trap: Ashoka's patronage was not restricted to Buddhism; certain Barabar caves were dedicated to Ajivikas.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, pp. 69–70; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 87–89 and 106–107; Jainpedia, Sacred Writings and illustrated Kalpa Sutra manuscript collections; Jinavani, Acharya Hemachandra; Gujarat Tourism, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill and Religious Sites; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
